CausalChain: NAFLD/obesity -> Enhanced de novo lipogenesis -> Accumulation of saturated fatty acids -> Shift in ceramide metabolism (↑C16-ceramide, ↓polyunsaturated ceramides via SphK2/CERT/CERS2 interplay) -> Impaired p53 activation & Enhanced NF-κB signaling -> Dysregulated bile acid receptor signaling (FXR/TGR5) -> Pro-inflammatory & immunosuppressive microenvironment -> Hepatocellular carcinoma development
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in patients with NAFLD and obesity, the increase in de novo lipogenesis produces an excess of saturated fatty acids that, through modulation of ceramide biosynthetic enzymes (including SphK2, CERT, and CERS2), skews ceramide metabolism toward elevated levels of C16-ceramide and diminished levels of polyunsaturated ceramide species. This altered ceramide profile disrupts the p53-mediated apoptotic pathway while simultaneously triggering NF-κB signaling and perturbing bile acid receptor functions (notably FXR and TGR5). These converging molecular events establish a chronic inflammatory and immune-suppressive hepatic microenvironment that predisposes to HCC initiation and progression. By employing advanced lipidomics and transcriptomics to map these changes in detail, along with CRISPR-based gene editing to selectively modulate key enzymes in the ceramide pathway, we can test whether restoring a balanced ceramide profile re-establishes apoptotic regulation and enhances tumor immune surveillance, thereby offering a novel precision therapeutic strategy against HCC.
Abstract: We propose that in NAFLD and obesity, heightened de novo lipogenesis not only elevates saturated fatty acid levels but also triggers a reprogramming of ceramide metabolism that is more complex than previously appreciated. Specifically, this metabolic shift, mediated through both fatty acid–driven changes and the interplay of enzymes such as SphK2, CERT, and CERS2, promotes an increase in pro-tumorigenic C16-ceramide and a decrease in polyunsaturated ceramide species. These alterations further disrupt p53‐mediated apoptotic responses and activate NF‐κB–dependent inflammatory pathways while also perturbing bile acid receptor signaling (e.g., FXR and TGR5). The resulting immune-suppressive, pro-inflammatory hepatic microenvironment fosters hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) development. Leveraging cutting-edge multi-omics—including advanced lipidomics, transcriptomics, and CRISPR-based gene editing—this hypothesis will be tested by precise quantification and targeted manipulation of ceramide biosynthetic enzymes to restore lipid homeostasis, re-establish apoptotic signaling, and reprogram the tumor microenvironment towards enhanced immune surveillance.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis centered solely on the role of increased de novo lipogenesis in shifting ceramide profiles (specifically increasing C16-ceramide while reducing polyunsaturated species) to disrupt p53 and activate NF-κB, thereby promoting HCC. The revised hypothesis expands on this causal chain by incorporating established enzymatic regulation (via SphK2, CERT, and CERS2) that modulates ceramide species, and by explicitly detailing the role of bile acid receptor signaling (FXR/TGR5) in the inflammatory cascade. Further, it leverages contemporary technologies such as advanced lipidomics, transcriptomics, and CRISPR gene editing to more precisely test and therapeutically target these molecular pathways. Each step of the original causal chain is thus refined: from metabolic dysregulation (NAFLD/obesity) to altered lipid profiles, impaired apoptotic and inflammatory signaling, and ultimately the development of a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment that drives HCC.
